title: Design functional enzymes to specification across reaction classes

concept.text: Conceptual synthesis: The innovation would let a researcher specify a chemical transformation and the required catalytic performance, then obtain an enzyme that carries out that reaction with useful activity and selectivity. Its defining ambition is breadth across mechanistically distinct reaction classes, including reactions for which no already optimized catalytic motif provides a starting point. Success would require an economical design-and-test process, with a disclosed experimental screening burden.

Conceptual synthesis: Predicting how a protein folds and designing a useful catalyst address different requirements. A folded structure describes an arrangement of atoms; a catalytic specification asks whether that arrangement enables the desired chemical transformation at an adequate rate and preferentially produces the intended outcome. Computational protein design, mechanistic chemistry and biocatalysis therefore meet in this concept, but a plausible structure alone would not demonstrate completion.

significance.text: Conditional synthesis: Reliable specification-to-enzyme design would make catalytic protein engineering substantially more programmable. Researchers could begin with a desired transformation and measurable performance requirements, expanding experimental access to catalysts beyond those available through existing enzymes or optimized motifs. The direct consequence would be a broader, more predictable ability to obtain and test useful catalysts.

Conditional synthesis: That capability could support industrial synthesis, environmental applications and medicines, but each would require further development. A catalyst that works in an experimental assay may still need process integration, suitable operating conditions and economical production. Environmental and medical uses would additionally depend on delivery, persistence, specificity and safety in their intended settings. These downstream benefits are possibilities, not demonstrated outcomes of the proposed innovation.

Interpretive synthesis: The analogy to programming is useful insofar as an explicit specification would guide construction and testing. It should not imply that every chemical reaction admits a practical enzyme solution, that performance can be guaranteed without experiments, or that demonstrations on a finite panel establish unrestricted generality. The revolutionary advance would be reliable performance across a demonstrated range of chemistries within stated practical limits.

missing_breakthrough.text: Conceptual synthesis: The missing capability is a reliable, economical route from a reaction specification to experimentally verified catalytic performance across diverse mechanisms. The central challenge is not simply producing a stable protein scaffold: the design must create an active site that supports the required chemistry and achieves the specified rate and selectivity. Cases without optimized catalytic templates are essential to the ambition because they test whether the method can establish a suitable catalytic arrangement rather than depend entirely on one already available.

Engineering synthesis: A specification-driven system would need to connect mechanistic reasoning to realizable protein designs, preserve the intended catalytic arrangement in the resulting protein, and predict which candidates will function under the specified assay conditions. It would also need to distinguish candidates that merely appear structurally plausible from those likely to satisfy catalytic requirements. These are an articulation of the proposed engineering problem; the supplied source content does not establish which barriers have been overcome or their relative difficulty.

Engineering synthesis: Practical generality also requires controlling the cost of finding successful designs. Large screening campaigns or extensive subsequent optimization could obscure how much useful performance came from the initial design method. A convincing advance therefore needs explicit accounting of computational candidate generation, experimental screening, unsuccessful designs and any optimization after initial testing. The supplied materials do not quantify an acceptable burden or define the boundary between a usable catalytic motif and an already optimized template.

current_state.text: The supplied research identifies Braun, Tripp et al., “Computational enzyme design by catalytic motif scaffolding,” with an online publication date of December 3, 2025 and DOI 10.1038/s41586-025-09747-9. It attributes designed catalysts for two reaction types using catalytic arrays to that work. These bibliographic details and the two-reaction scope are retained as reported information: the supplied review could not verify them against article content.

According to the supplied review, the retained PubMed artifact contains only a cookie-access challenge, without the bibliographic record, abstract, methods or results. The source index records a 153-character, untruncated extraction retrieved on November 11, 2026. An untruncated access-challenge page is not a complete scientific document, so it cannot substantiate the reported catalytic results or establish the article’s identity and publication date. This access limitation does not show that the reported work is false.

Evidence-bounded synthesis: If confirmed, the reported work would represent progress in motif-based enzyme design. Demonstrations using catalytic arrays for two reaction types would still leave a separate question about performance across diverse mechanisms, especially where suitable motifs are unavailable. The supplied materials establish neither achievement of the broader specification-to-enzyme capability nor its field-wide absence.

Assessment limitation: No bounded freshness-search record was supplied for the review’s November 1, 2026 assessment date. The later retrieval timestamp does not supply such a search or establish the state of the field on either date. The research also reports that the publisher page could not be opened, but the review found no retained documentation of that attempt. Neither missing record supports an additional conclusion about scientific progress.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: Use a blinded panel of independently selected reactions spanning mechanistically distinct classes. Before designs are submitted, specify the required activity, selectivity and operating conditions for each reaction. Include reactions lacking optimized active-site templates, and disclose how that condition is defined and checked. Independent selection would reduce selection bias, while prespecified requirements would make functional success assessable.
completion_criteria.label: Blinded reaction panel spans mechanistic classes with prespecified catalytic requirements

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundary: Set a numerical limit on the experimental screening burden before testing, and report the complete burden alongside successes and failures. Disclose how many candidates were generated, how many were experimentally tested, and whether further optimization was needed to meet the specification. The original proposal calls for a small burden, but no numerical threshold is supplied; any adopted limit would be an evaluation choice rather than an established standard.
completion_criteria.label: Prespecified screening limit and complete experimental burden reporting

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirement: Independent laboratories should reproduce catalytic performance using disclosed sequences, production procedures, assay conditions and measurement methods. Controls should distinguish the intended catalytic activity from background reactions or other assay effects. Results should include unsuccessful reaction classes and the conditions under which otherwise successful designs fail, allowing readers to assess reproducibility and practical boundaries.
completion_criteria.label: Independent laboratories reproduce catalytic performance and report failure conditions

completion_criteria.text: Proposed interpretation: Completion should mean convincing, reproducible breadth across the declared panel within the declared performance and resource limits. A finite panel cannot establish literal universality. Laboratory success would also remain distinct from readiness for an industrial process, environmental deployment or medical use, each of which would require application-specific demonstrations.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible panel breadth meets declared performance and resource limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: BIO-03, “Predict the effects of genome changes across biological contexts,” overlaps through the relationship between sequence changes and function, but asks for prediction of biological consequences rather than construction of catalysts to reaction specifications. BIO-14, “Establish causal functions for noncoding elements and poorly understood proteins,” concerns discovering what existing biological components do; BIO-05 concerns designing proteins to perform a chosen catalytic task. Insights could inform each other without making the completion criteria interchangeable.

Roster-based synthesis: BIO-04, “Create an experimentally predictive virtual cell,” and BIO-10, “Observe molecular state and dynamics inside living cells at scale,” could help evaluate how designed enzymes behave in cellular settings. BIO-05 can nevertheless be demonstrated through defined catalytic assays without a whole-cell model or comprehensive cellular observation. BIO-01, “Build an autonomously reproducing cell from defined components,” could potentially use designed catalysts, but requires integrated cellular reproduction beyond the scope of enzyme design.

Roster-based synthesis: BIO-08, “Make major cereal crops reliably obtain most of their nitrogen biologically,” is a possible application neighbor where catalytic engineering might contribute to a larger biological system. Producing an enzyme would not by itself establish reliable nitrogen provision in crops. BIO-15, “Deliver programmable genome editors selectively to diverse cells in the body,” shares an interest in programmable molecular tools, but selective delivery across tissues is a separate capability from catalytic design.

Roster-based synthesis: BIO-02, “Demonstrate a plausible chemical transition from nonlife to evolution,” and BIO-12, “Explain how biological homochirality could emerge and persist,” overlap with questions of catalysis and chemical selectivity. Engineered enzymes might provide experimental tools, but their deliberate design would not establish a historically plausible origin-of-life pathway or explain the emergence of biological handedness. BIO-11, concerning the origin of eukaryotic cells, likewise asks for an evolutionary reconstruction rather than a general catalyst-design method.

unresolved_issues: The article’s identity, author attribution, online date, two reported reaction types and catalytic-array results remain unverified against scientific document content in the supplied materials.

The supplied evidence does not establish whether broader specification-driven enzyme design has been demonstrated elsewhere or characterize the field comprehensively as of November 1 or November 11, 2026.
The research reports a publisher-page access failure, but the supplied review found no retained documentation confirming the attempt.
An operational evaluation still needs reaction-selection rules, numerical activity and selectivity requirements, assay conditions, and a quantified experimental screening budget.
The evaluation must define optimized catalytic templates and distinguish initial design performance from gains obtained through subsequent screening or optimization.
No review recommendation was rejected; the proposed reproducibility and practical-boundary details are explicitly presented as synthesis rather than sourced standards.

brief.title: Custom proteins for chosen chemical reactions
possible: A researcher could specify a chemical reaction, how fast it should run and which product it should favour, then obtain an enzyme—a protein that speeds up that reaction. This would work across reactions with different underlying chemistry, including those without an already optimized starting design.
why: Chemists could start with the transformation they need, rather than search for an existing enzyme they can adapt. A predictable way to obtain useful enzymes could widen the reactions available for manufacturing, environmental applications and medicines.

sources.who: Markus Braun, Adrian Tripp and collaborators
sources.showed: Their Riff-Diff method built enzymes for two chemically distinct reactions around previously optimized active sites—the pockets where reactions happen. Some matched enzymes improved through laboratory mutation and testing.
sources.quote: We show that in both cases, it is possible to generate catalysts that exhibit activities rivalling those optimized by in vitro evolution, along with exquisite stereoselectivity.
sources.cited_for: Useful activity and preference for a particular product can survive placement of an optimized active site into a newly designed protein.
sources.not_established: This does not establish design across diverse chemistry without optimized starting sites.

sources.who: Jarrid Rector-Brooks, Théophile Lambert, Marta Skreta and collaborators
sources.showed: In a preprint, the team reports that DISCO designed active enzymes without fixing the protein's catalytic groups beforehand. Some outperformed enzymes improved through laboratory mutation and testing, called directed evolution.
sources.quote:
Random mutagenesis of a selected design further confirmed that enzyme activity can be improved
through directed evolution.
sources.cited_for: Functional enzymes can emerge without a predefined arrangement of catalytic protein groups.
sources.not_established: The demonstrated reactions share a chemical approach; they do not establish breadth across distinct mechanisms or independent reproduction.

sources.who: Donghyo Kim, Seth M. Woodbury, Woody Ahern and collaborators
sources.showed: The team designed enzymes that use zinc to help water break a chemical bond. They obtained high activity without experimental optimization.
sources.quote:
the crystal structure of 
the most active design is very close to the design model
sources.cited_for: A calculated active-site arrangement can become an accurately built, active enzyme.
sources.not_established: Success with this reaction does not establish reliable performance across different chemical mechanisms.

sources.who: Woody Ahern, Jason Yim, Doug Tischer and collaborators
sources.showed: RFdiffusion2 built proteins around specified catalytic atoms without requiring their positions along the protein chain in advance. Experiments found active enzymes across distinct mechanisms.
sources.quote:
We
further design enzymes for three distinct catalytic mechanisms
sources.cited_for: The same design method can produce active enzymes across different mechanisms.
sources.not_established: Finding activity does not establish that independently chosen reactions meet advance performance targets within a fixed testing budget.

sources.showed: The team designed efficient enzymes for a model chemical reaction without repeated screening of mutation libraries. Their approach assembled protein fragments and optimized the designs computationally.
sources.quote:
The most efficient shows more 
than 140 mutations from any natural protein, including a novel active site.
sources.cited_for: Computational design can deliver useful activity without extensive experimental optimization.
sources.not_established: The demonstration covers a model reaction, leaving breadth across reaction classes unresolved.

shown: Ahern and colleagues found active enzymes across three distinct mechanisms using RFdiffusion2. Braun and colleagues obtained strong activity by building around optimized catalytic arrangements.

DISCO goes further in another direction: it produces active enzymes without predefined catalytic protein groups. Together, these results demonstrate pieces of the capability, but do not yet demonstrate reliable design to specification across a broadly chosen reaction panel.
missing: A reliable route from a reaction specification to the required speed and product preference across distinct chemical mechanisms remains to be demonstrated.
Broad success must include reactions without optimized starting sites and stay within a declared, economical testing budget.
Independent laboratories still need to reproduce performance across the chosen reaction panel and establish where the designs fail.

milestones.label: Success on independently chosen reactions with advance targets
milestones.explanation: A blinded, independently selected panel would have to span different mechanisms, set performance targets in advance and include reactions without optimized templates. This would test breadth with less selection bias.

milestones.label: Success within a declared testing budget
milestones.explanation: Testing would have to stay below a numerical limit set beforehand, with all generated candidates, experiments, failures and later optimization reported. This would reveal the practical cost of obtaining useful enzymes.

milestones.label: Independent reproduction and clear failure conditions
milestones.explanation: Independent laboratories would have to reproduce activity with controls that exclude background reactions and report unsuccessful cases and failure conditions. This would establish reliability and practical boundaries.

milestones.label: Reproducible breadth within declared limits
milestones.explanation: The panel would have to reproducibly meet its declared performance and resource limits. This would establish a bounded design capability, while industrial, environmental and medical uses would require further demonstrations.

uncertain: How broad must the reaction panel be to demonstrate useful generality?
What testing budget and performance thresholds would make the method practical?
Where should the boundary fall between an acceptable starting arrangement and an already optimized catalytic template?

page.title: Enzyme design to specification across catalytic mechanisms
page.definition: A design method produces enzymes—proteins that accelerate chemical reactions—from a specified transformation, reaction conditions, catalytic rate and product selectivity. It works across distinct catalytic mechanisms, including reactions without a pre-optimized protein active site.

goal.need: Two zinc-hydrolase campaigns each tested 96 designs; their best efficiencies are shown below. EBRC targets routine design above 10⁵ M⁻¹ s⁻¹ in catalytic efficiency, kcat/KM, the low-substrate rate constant. A Kemp eliminase has exceeded that value. The remaining capability is control of requested catalytic performance across mechanisms.

figures.caption: Designed zinc-catalysed ester hydrolysis, published on 3 December 2025.
figures.note: Substrate: 4-methylumbelliferyl phenylacetate. Values are means ± standard deviations from three independent measurements.

statements.context: The roadmap identifies this as a major goal of computational enzyme design.

statements.quote: Thus, it is necessary to advance our ability to design efficient enzymes using a one-shot approach.

completion.title: Designed enzymes meet prospective catalytic specifications across distinct reaction mechanisms.
completion.criterion: In a prospective experimental test, one design method produces enzymes for user-selected reactions spanning distinct catalytic mechanisms, including a reaction without a pre-optimized protein active site. Each enzyme meets numerical rate and product-selectivity specifications under conditions and within a screening budget fixed before design. An independent laboratory reproduces the specified performance. Reaction-specific tolerances and the screening budget belong to the test protocol; no field-wide numerical panel size, hit rate or budget is established here.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; provisional operational test derived from the quoted enzyme-design goals.
completion.basis: Searches of EBRC's 2019 and 2020 roadmaps and web searches for DARPA targets, NIST benchmarks and enzyme-design prize rules located no operational test combining reaction breadth, specified activity, selectivity and screening burden. EBRC publishes an activity threshold and a kinetic-control goal, but no complete cross-mechanism acceptance protocol. This provisional Atlas test operationalises those goals without assigning unsupported universal numbers.

milestones.title: A designed enzyme completes repeated catalytic turnovers on its target substrate.
milestones.criterion: Repeated product formation above matched background establishes catalytic turnover; a single covalent reaction does not. Lauko et al. found turnover in 2 of 132 third-round serine-hydrolase designs in their Science article dated 18 April 2025. RFdiffusion2 tested 48 cysteine-hydrolase designs and demonstrated multiple turnover. Riff-Diff produced retro-aldol and Morita–Baylis–Hillman catalysts. DISCO tested 90 designs across four carbene-transfer reactions in its 6 April 2026 preprint, which is not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: Experimental enzymology's distinction between single-turnover reactivity and repeated catalysis, applied by Lauko et al. to designed serine hydrolases and by the cited design studies to other mechanisms.
milestones.threshold_quote: Previous efforts to design catalytic triad-based designs have failed to achieve multiple turnover;

milestones.title: A de novo enzyme exceeds a catalytic efficiency of 10⁵ M⁻¹ s⁻¹.
milestones.criterion: For a stated substrate and assay conditions, measured kcat/KM must exceed 100,000 M⁻¹ s⁻¹. This adopts the activity component of EBRC's routine-design target. Published on 18 June 2025, Listov et al. reported Des27.7 F113L at 123,000 M⁻¹ s⁻¹ and kcat 30 s⁻¹ for 5-nitrobenzisoxazole at 25 °C and pH 7.3. The work tested 73 initial designs before computationally redesigning selected candidates; main-text kinetic measurements used biological duplicates or triplicates. This satisfies the single-reaction activity bar.
milestones.set_by: Engineering Biology Research Consortium, 2019 roadmap; numerical activity component of its routine enzyme-design target, applied here to an individual enzyme.

milestones.title: A de novo enzyme meets kinetic values and tolerances specified before design for a new reaction.
milestones.criterion: For one new chemistry/substrate pair, an experimentally produced de novo enzyme meets kcat and KM values and acceptance tolerances fixed before design. Here kcat is the saturated turnover rate in s⁻¹ and KM is the substrate concentration in M giving half-maximal rate under Michaelis–Menten conditions. EBRC names controlled kinetic parameters as a goal but supplies no tolerance. Riff-Diff and DISCO report catalytic activities, not a prospective test of prescribed kcat and KM; DISCO is not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: Technology Atlas; operationalisation of EBRC's 2020 kinetic-control goal. Searches of the roadmaps and experimental benchmarks located no published acceptance tolerance for that goal.

not_found: No external acceptance test combining reaction breadth, prospective activity and selectivity specifications, and a screening budget was located.
No numerical acceptance tolerance for EBRC's goal of precisely engineered Km and kcat was located.
